questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a chemical bond?
questions.correct: An attraction between atomic nuclei and electrons that holds atoms together
wrong: A collision that transfers protons between atoms
A force that exists only between neutral atoms
An attraction between nuclei without any role for electrons
questions.explanation: Chemical bonding results from attractions involving positively charged nuclei and electrons, which can lower the energy of the atoms together.

questions.prompt: Which set lists the three broad bond types discussed in the lesson?
questions.explanation: The three broad types are ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding. Polar and nonpolar describe covalent bonding or molecular polarity.

questions.prompt: What happens to valence electrons in a typical ionic bond?
questions.correct: They are transferred from one atom to another
wrong: They are shared equally by both atoms
They remain only on the nonmetal before bonding
They are converted into protons in the crystal
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer, producing oppositely charged ions that attract one another.

questions.prompt: What happens to valence electrons in a covalent bond?
wrong: They are completely transferred to the more electronegative atom
They are removed from both atoms
They are confined to a metal lattice
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds form when atoms share valence electrons.

questions.prompt: Which pairing most commonly forms an ionic compound?
questions.correct: A metal cation and a nonmetal anion
wrong: A metal anion and a nonmetal cation
questions.explanation: Metals usually lose electrons to form cations, while nonmetals gain electrons to form anions.

questions.prompt: During ionic bond formation, a metal atom usually ____.
questions.correct: loses electrons and becomes a cation
wrong: gains electrons and becomes a cation
gains protons and becomes an anion
questions.explanation: Losing negatively charged electrons leaves a metal with a net positive charge, so it becomes a cation.

questions.prompt: During ionic bond formation, a nonmetal atom usually ____.
questions.correct: gains electrons and becomes an anion
wrong: loses electrons and becomes an anion
shares only protons and becomes neutral
loses neutrons and becomes a cation
questions.explanation: Gaining negatively charged electrons gives a nonmetal a net negative charge, producing an anion.

questions.prompt: What directly holds the ions together in an ionic solid?
questions.correct: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
wrong: Equal sharing of one electron pair
Repulsion between ions of the same charge
A directional overlap of metal orbitals only
questions.explanation: Ionic solids are held by the attraction between positive cations and negative anions.

questions.prompt: Why do ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points?
questions.correct: A large amount of energy is needed to overcome attractions in the ionic lattice
wrong: Their molecules have especially weak intermolecular forces
Their ions share electrons in double bonds
Their electrons move freely between isolated molecules
questions.explanation: The repeating ionic lattice contains strong electrostatic attractions that require substantial energy to break.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the structure of a typical ionic solid?
questions.correct: A three-dimensional crystal lattice of repeating ions
wrong: A chain of identical neutral atoms
A two-dimensional sheet of shared electron pairs
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds form extended three-dimensional lattices rather than individual molecules.

questions.prompt: Why can an ionic crystal be hard but brittle?
questions.correct: A shift can bring like-charged ions together, causing strong repulsion and cleavage
wrong: Its ions become neutral when the crystal is struck
Its electron pairs flow away from the point of impact
Its covalent bonds gradually stretch instead of breaking
questions.explanation: When lattice layers shift, similarly charged ions may line up. Their repulsion can split the crystal.

questions.prompt: When does an ionic compound usually conduct electricity?
questions.correct: When molten or dissolved in water, because its ions can move
wrong: Only as a solid, because the lattice is rigid
Only as a gas, because the ions become covalent
In every state, because all electrons are delocalized
questions.explanation: Molten and aqueous ionic compounds contain mobile ions that can carry electric current.

questions.prompt: Why does a solid ionic compound usually not conduct electricity?
questions.correct: Its ions are fixed in place in the crystal lattice
wrong: Its bonds are all nonpolar covalent
questions.explanation: Ions are present in a solid ionic compound, but they cannot move through the rigid lattice.

questions.prompt: Which solvent would most ionic compounds be more likely to dissolve in?
wrong: A pure metal melt, because it is conductive
questions.explanation: Polar water molecules can surround and stabilize separated ions, so ionic compounds are often water-soluble.

questions.prompt: A metallic bond is most characteristic of which substance?
questions.correct: A sample made only of metal atoms, such as solid silver
wrong: A compound of sodium and chlorine
A molecule made of carbon and hydrogen
A mixture of a nonmetal gas and water
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding occurs between metal atoms in pure metals and metal alloys.

questions.prompt: Which pair is most likely joined primarily by covalent bonding?
wrong: A metal atom and a nonmetal atom
A metal cation and a nonmetal anion
Two ions with opposite charges in a lattice
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds commonly form between nonmetal atoms by sharing valence electrons.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes covalent bonds directional?
questions.correct: Shared electron pairs are located between particular atoms
wrong: Cations and anions attract equally in all directions
The atoms must form a cubic crystal lattice
Valence electrons are transferred completely away from both atoms
questions.explanation: Because the shared electrons lie between specific nuclei, covalent bonds give molecules definite arrangements and shapes.

questions.prompt: Why do many covalent compounds have lower melting points than ionic compounds?
questions.correct: The attractions between separate molecules are often relatively weak
wrong: Covalent bonds inside molecules are always weak
They contain mobile ions in a lattice
Their atoms have no valence electrons
questions.explanation: The covalent bonds within a molecule can be strong, but the intermolecular attractions between molecules are often weaker.

questions.prompt: Why are many simple covalent compounds poor electrical conductors?
questions.correct: They usually lack mobile ions or freely moving electrons
wrong: Their valence electrons are all transferred to water
questions.explanation: Simple molecular substances generally have no mobile charged particles available to carry current.

questions.prompt: Which physical description is most typical of many molecular covalent substances?
questions.correct: Gases, liquids, or soft solids with relatively low melting points
wrong: Malleable metal solids with a sea of electrons
Always rigid crystals that conduct as solids
questions.explanation: Many covalent molecular substances are gases, liquids, or soft solids because of comparatively weak intermolecular forces.

questions.prompt: What is valency?
questions.correct: An atom's combining capacity based on electrons it can lose, gain, or share
wrong: The total number of protons in an atom
The mass of the outermost electron shell
The number of neutrons transferred in a reaction
questions.explanation: Valency describes how many electrons an atom tends to lose, gain, or share to become stable.

questions.prompt: In a Lewis electron-dot symbol, the dots represent ____.
questions.explanation: Lewis dots show only valence electrons, the electrons most involved in bonding.

questions.prompt: For a representative element, what does the ones digit of its group number indicate in Lewis-dot work?
wrong: The number of occupied energy levels
The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of bonds it must always form
questions.explanation: For main-group elements, the ones digit of the group number corresponds to the number of valence electrons.

questions.prompt: When placing dots around a Lewis symbol, what is the usual first step?
questions.correct: Place one dot on each side before pairing any dots
wrong: Place all dots as pairs on the top side first
Draw bond lines before placing any electrons
Put every dot inside the element symbol
questions.explanation: Lewis-dot symbols distribute single electrons around the four sides before electrons are paired.

questions.prompt: Which atom usually needs only two electrons for a filled first shell?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen follows the duet rule: its first energy level is filled by two electrons.

questions.prompt: Which atom is commonly taught as an octet-rule exception that can be stable with six electrons?
questions.explanation: Boron is commonly electron-deficient in compounds such as BCl₃ and can be stable with six surrounding electrons.

questions.prompt: In a covalent Lewis structure, which atom is usually chosen as the central atom?
questions.correct: The atom with more unpaired electrons, often carbon when it is present
wrong: Hydrogen, because it forms one bond
Fluorine, because it is highly electronegative
The terminal atom with the fewest unpaired electrons
questions.explanation: The central atom generally has more unpaired electrons; carbon is normally central when it is in the formula.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct for a molecule with only two atoms, such as HCl?
wrong: The more electronegative atom is always central
The atom written first is always central
questions.explanation: A diatomic molecule has only two atoms, so neither is considered a central atom.

questions.prompt: How many valence electrons are available for the Lewis structure of H₂O?
questions.explanation: Each H supplies 1 valence electron and O supplies 6, giving 1 + 1 + 6 = 8.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are needed for H₂O when each H follows the duet rule and O follows the octet rule?
questions.explanation: The two H atoms need 2 each and oxygen needs 8, so the total needed is 12 electrons.

questions.prompt: In the ANS method, what does the difference between needed and available electrons tell you?
questions.correct: How many electrons must be shared in bonds
wrong: How many protons must be transferred
How many lone pairs must be removed
How many energy levels the molecule has
questions.explanation: Needed minus available equals the number of electrons that must be shared to satisfy the electron requirements.

questions.prompt: How is the number of covalent bonds found after calculating shared electrons in the ANS method?
questions.correct: Divide the number of shared electrons by 2
wrong: Multiply the number of shared electrons by 2
Subtract 2 from the number of shared electrons
questions.explanation: Each covalent bond consists of one shared pair, or two electrons.

questions.prompt: How many bonding pairs are present in a double bond?
questions.explanation: A double bond contains two shared electron pairs, which is four shared electrons.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in a triple bond?
questions.explanation: A triple bond has three shared electron pairs, for a total of six shared electrons.

questions.prompt: How many single bonds are shown in the usual Lewis structure of CH₄?
questions.explanation: Carbon is central in methane and forms four single C—H bonds.

questions.prompt: How many lone-pair electrons remain on nitrogen in the usual Lewis structure of NH₃?
questions.explanation: NH₃ has three N—H bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen, which contains two electrons.

questions.prompt: Which Lewis description matches CO₂?
questions.correct: Carbon is central with two double bonds to oxygen
wrong: Oxygen is central with two single bonds to carbon
Carbon is central with four single bonds to oxygen
The atoms form an ionic lattice of C⁴⁺ and O²⁻
questions.explanation: CO₂ is represented as O=C=O, with carbon in the center and two C=O double bonds.

questions.prompt: How many electrons remain unshared after the bonding in the Lewis structure of CO₂ is completed?
questions.explanation: CO₂ has 16 available valence electrons. Eight are in the two double bonds, leaving eight as oxygen lone-pair electrons.

questions.prompt: Why does BCl₃ have only three B—Cl bonds in its common Lewis structure?
questions.correct: Boron can be stable with six electrons rather than a full octet
wrong: Chlorine never forms more than one lone pair
Boron must have a complete duet like hydrogen
The compound is ionic rather than covalent
questions.explanation: Boron is an octet-rule exception; three bonds place six electrons around B in BCl₃.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes a molecular formula from a structural formula?
questions.correct: A molecular formula gives atom counts, while a structural formula shows bonding arrangement
wrong: A molecular formula shows bonds, while a structural formula gives only counts
Both always show the same electron pairs
Only a structural formula can name the elements present
questions.explanation: For example, NH₃ gives the composition, while a structural formula shows how N is connected to the three H atoms.

questions.prompt: A bond has an electronegativity difference greater than about 1.8. How is it classified in this lesson?
questions.explanation: The lesson uses a difference above 1.8 as the ionic range.

questions.prompt: A bond has an electronegativity difference of 1.1. How is it classified in this lesson?
questions.explanation: A difference from about 0.50 to 1.79 is classified as polar covalent in the lesson.

questions.prompt: A bond has an electronegativity difference of 0.3. How is it classified in this lesson?
questions.explanation: A difference below about 0.49 is classified as nonpolar covalent because the electrons are shared nearly evenly.

questions.prompt: As an electronegativity difference moves closer to 2.0, the bond generally has ____.
wrong: less attraction between nuclei and electrons
questions.explanation: A larger electronegativity difference means more unequal electron attraction and more ionic character.

questions.prompt: Which bond is expected to be the most polar based on the lesson's sample differences?
questions.explanation: The sample values show H—F with the largest difference (about 1.9), larger than H—Cl, C—H, or N—N.

questions.prompt: Which bond is nonpolar because its two atoms have the same electronegativity?
questions.explanation: Atoms in a Cl₂ bond attract the shared electrons equally, so the bond is nonpolar.

questions.prompt: Can a molecule with polar bonds still be a nonpolar molecule?
questions.correct: Yes, if its bond dipoles cancel because of a symmetrical arrangement
wrong: No, one polar bond always makes the whole molecule polar
Only if it contains an ionic bond
Only if every atom has a lone pair
questions.explanation: Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of all bond dipoles, not on a single bond alone.

questions.prompt: Why is CO₂ usually classified as a nonpolar molecule even though each C=O bond is polar?
questions.correct: Its linear, symmetrical arrangement lets the two bond dipoles cancel
wrong: Carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativity
The molecule contains no shared electrons
Its double bonds are ionic instead of covalent
questions.explanation: The two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions in linear CO₂, so the overall dipole is zero.

questions.prompt: Why is H₂O a polar molecule?
questions.correct: Its bent shape prevents the O—H bond dipoles from canceling
wrong: Oxygen transfers both electrons completely to hydrogen
Its electron pairs form a linear arrangement
questions.explanation: Water's bent molecular geometry creates a net dipole, so the molecule is polar.

questions.prompt: Which molecule is a good example of a symmetrical, nonpolar molecule from the lesson?
questions.explanation: CCl₄ has a symmetrical tetrahedral arrangement of identical C—Cl bonds, so its bond dipoles cancel.

questions.prompt: Which molecule is polar because its atoms are not arranged symmetrically around the central atom?
questions.explanation: CH₃Cl has different atoms around carbon, so its bond dipoles do not cancel completely.

questions.prompt: What is molecular geometry?
questions.correct: The three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule
wrong: The total mass of the atoms in a molecule
The two-dimensional order of element symbols in a formula
The number of electrons transferred in an ionic bond
questions.explanation: Molecular geometry describes a molecule's 3-D atomic arrangement, which affects its properties and polarity.

questions.prompt: What does VSEPR stand for?
questions.explanation: VSEPR predicts molecular shape by considering repulsions among electron pairs around a central atom.

questions.prompt: According to VSEPR theory, electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to ____.
questions.correct: minimize repulsion by staying as far apart as possible
wrong: form a flat shape in every molecule
line up only with lone pairs
questions.explanation: Electron pairs repel one another, so they orient in space to reduce those repulsions.

questions.prompt: For VSEPR counting, how is a double or triple bond treated around the central atom?
wrong: As two or three separate electron domains
questions.explanation: A multiple bond contains more electrons, but it occupies one region of electron density for basic VSEPR shape counting.

questions.prompt: Which electron pairs must be counted around a central atom for VSEPR?
questions.correct: Both bonding pairs and lone pairs
questions.explanation: Both bonding electron regions and lone pairs repel and affect the arrangement around the central atom.

questions.prompt: How does a lone pair generally repel compared with a bonding pair?
wrong: Exactly the same in every case
Not at all because it is unshared
questions.explanation: Lone pairs are concentrated closer to the central atom and repel bonding pairs more strongly.

questions.prompt: In the notation ABₓ, what does A represent?
wrong: A lone pair on the central atom
questions.explanation: In VSEPR notation, A is the central atom and B represents atoms attached to it.

questions.prompt: In the notation ABₓEᵧ, what does E represent?
questions.correct: A lone pair on the central atom
wrong: An electron transferred from a metal
questions.explanation: E indicates lone-pair electron domains located on the central atom.

questions.prompt: A central atom with two electron domains and no lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: Two electron domains arrange opposite each other, producing a linear geometry.

questions.prompt: What is the ideal bond angle for a linear molecule such as BeCl₂?
questions.explanation: Two electron domains are farthest apart when separated by 180°.

questions.prompt: A central atom with three electron domains and no lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: Three bonding regions with no lone pairs arrange in one plane as trigonal planar.

questions.prompt: What is the ideal bond angle in a trigonal planar molecule such as BF₃?
questions.explanation: Three electron domains in a plane are equally spaced by 120°.

questions.prompt: A central atom with four electron domains and no lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: Four bonding domains with no lone pairs arrange tetrahedrally, as in CH₄.

questions.prompt: What is the ideal bond angle in a tetrahedral molecule such as CH₄?
questions.explanation: Four electron domains in a tetrahedral arrangement have ideal angles of about 109.5°.

questions.prompt: A central atom with five electron domains and no lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: Five bonding domains arrange as trigonal bipyramidal, as in PCl₅.

questions.prompt: Which pair of ideal angles occurs in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement?
questions.explanation: Equatorial positions are 120° apart, and axial positions are 90° from equatorial positions.

questions.prompt: A central atom with six electron domains and no lone pairs has what molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: Six bonding domains arrange octahedrally, as in SF₆.

questions.prompt: What is the ideal angle between adjacent bonds in an octahedral molecule such as SF₆?
questions.explanation: In an octahedral arrangement, adjacent bonds are 90° apart; opposite bonds are 180° apart.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match SO₂ in the lesson table?
questions.explanation: SO₂ has three electron domains around sulfur: two bonding domains and one lone pair, giving AB₂E and a bent molecular shape.

questions.prompt: What is the electron-pair arrangement around the central atom in SO₂?
questions.explanation: SO₂ has three electron domains, so its electron-pair arrangement is trigonal planar even though its molecular geometry is bent.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match NH₃?
questions.explanation: NH₃ has three N—H bonding domains and one lone pair, so its molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.prompt: What is the electron-pair arrangement around nitrogen in NH₃?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen in NH₃ has four electron domains: three bonding domains and one lone pair. The electron-pair arrangement is tetrahedral.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match H₂O?
questions.explanation: Water has two O—H bonding domains and two lone pairs on oxygen, giving AB₂E₂ and a bent molecular geometry.

questions.prompt: What is the electron-pair arrangement around oxygen in H₂O?
questions.explanation: Oxygen in H₂O has four electron domains in total, so its electron-pair arrangement is tetrahedral.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match SF₄?
questions.explanation: SF₄ has five electron domains around sulfur: four bonding domains and one lone pair. Its molecular geometry is seesaw.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match ClF₃?
questions.explanation: ClF₃ has five electron domains with three bonding pairs and two lone pairs, producing a T-shaped molecular geometry.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match I₃⁻ in the lesson table?
questions.explanation: I₃⁻ has five electron domains around the central iodine: two bonding domains and three lone pairs. The remaining bonds are opposite, making it linear.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match BrF₅?
questions.explanation: BrF₅ has six electron domains with five bonding domains and one lone pair, giving a square pyramidal geometry.

questions.prompt: Which VSEPR notation and shape match XeF₄?
questions.explanation: XeF₄ has six electron domains. Four fluorines remain in a square plane while two lone pairs occupy opposite positions.

questions.prompt: Why is the molecular geometry of NH₃ not called tetrahedral?
questions.correct: One of nitrogen's four electron domains is a lone pair, not a bonded atom
wrong: Nitrogen has only three electron domains
Hydrogen atoms cannot form a tetrahedral arrangement
questions.explanation: NH₃ has a tetrahedral electron-pair arrangement, but molecular geometry describes atom positions only, so it is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.prompt: Why is the molecular geometry of H₂O not called tetrahedral?
questions.correct: Two of oxygen's four electron domains are lone pairs, leaving two bonded atoms in a bent shape
wrong: Water has only two total electron domains
questions.explanation: Water has a tetrahedral electron-pair arrangement, but only the two O—H bonds count for molecular geometry, giving bent.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has the same electron-pair arrangement as CH₄ but a different molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: Both CH₄ and NH₃ have four electron domains (tetrahedral arrangement), but NH₃ has a lone pair and is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has trigonal planar electron-pair arrangement but bent molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: SO₂ has two bonding domains and one lone pair around sulfur, so it is trigonal planar by electron arrangement and bent by molecular geometry.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has octahedral electron-pair arrangement but square planar molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: XeF₄ has six electron domains, including two opposite lone pairs, leaving four fluorines in a square planar arrangement.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair arrangement but T-shaped molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: ClF₃ has five electron domains; three bonds and two lone pairs give the T-shaped molecular geometry.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair arrangement but seesaw molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: SF₄ has five electron domains with one lone pair, producing a seesaw molecular geometry.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has octahedral electron-pair arrangement but square pyramidal molecular geometry?
questions.explanation: BrF₅ has six electron domains around bromine. One is a lone pair, leaving five fluorines in a square pyramidal shape.

questions.prompt: How many electron domains surround the central atom in PCl₅?
questions.explanation: PCl₅ has five P—Cl bonding domains and no lone pairs on phosphorus in the VSEPR model used here.

questions.prompt: How many electron domains surround the central atom in SF₆?
questions.explanation: SF₆ has six S—F bonding domains around the sulfur atom.

questions.prompt: How many electron domains surround the central atom in NH₃?
questions.explanation: NH₃ has three bonding domains and one lone-pair domain, totaling four electron domains.

questions.prompt: How many electron domains surround the central atom in H₂O?
questions.explanation: H₂O has two bonding domains and two lone-pair domains around oxygen, totaling four.

questions.prompt: How many electron domains surround the central atom in CO₂ for VSEPR purposes?
questions.explanation: Each C=O double bond counts as one electron domain, so carbon in CO₂ has two domains.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares electron-pair arrangement and molecular geometry?
questions.correct: Electron-pair arrangement counts lone pairs; molecular geometry describes only atom positions
wrong: They always have exactly the same name
Molecular geometry counts only lone pairs
questions.explanation: The two descriptions match when there are no central lone pairs, but they differ when lone pairs are present.

questions.prompt: When will electron-pair arrangement and molecular geometry have the same name?
questions.correct: When the central atom has no lone pairs
wrong: When the molecule contains a double bond
When the central atom has exactly one lone pair
questions.explanation: Without central lone pairs, every electron domain corresponds to a bonded atom, so the two descriptions coincide.

questions.prompt: Which shape is expected for a central atom with three bonded atoms and one lone pair?
questions.explanation: Three bonding domains plus one lone pair is AB₃E: tetrahedral electron arrangement and trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

questions.prompt: Which shape is expected for a central atom with two bonded atoms and two lone pairs?
questions.explanation: Two bonding domains and two lone pairs is AB₂E₂, which gives a bent molecular shape.

questions.prompt: Which shape is expected for a central atom with two bonded atoms and three lone pairs?
questions.explanation: AB₂E₃ has a trigonal bipyramidal electron arrangement. The three lone pairs leave the two bonds opposite each other, making it linear.

questions.prompt: Which shape is expected for a central atom with four bonded atoms and two lone pairs?
questions.explanation: AB₄E₂ has an octahedral electron arrangement; the two lone pairs occupy opposite positions, leaving a square planar molecular geometry.

questions.prompt: What should you draw first before determining a molecule's VSEPR shape?
wrong: A periodic-table group number with no electrons
questions.explanation: A Lewis structure reveals the bonding and lone pairs needed to count electron domains and predict molecular geometry.
